snip.t: Co-trimoxazole is contraindicated in severe hypersensitivity reactions.
*Pruritic papular eruption (PPE):* Symmetrical, intensely itchy papules on extremities caused by hypersensitivity to insect bites in immune-dysregulated hosts.
Atopy (type 1 hypersensitivity) in most childhood and allergic asthma.

Lymphatic drainage of the lung – peribronchovascular and subpleural lymphatics: Impaired drainage from chronic inflammation leads to interstitial oedema and facilitates deposition of fibrotic tissue; also a route for antigen presentation in hypersensitivity pneumonitis.
| Known cause | Occupational (silica, asbestos, coal), drugs (amiodarone, methotrexate, nitrofurantoin, bleomycin), radiation, hypersensitivity pneumonitis (farmer's lung, bird fancier's lung) |

Immune complex formation in the interstitium – Th1‑mediated granulomatous response: Organic antigens (mould spores, bird proteins) trigger type III/IV hypersensitivity → hypersensitivity pneumonitis with lymphocytic alveolitis, granulomas, and eventual fibrosis.
Hypersensitivity pneumonitis: immune reaction to organic dusts (see also the ILD note).

qs.q: A patient experiences an acute asthmatic bronchospasm triggered by allergen exposure, mediated by specific immunoglobulins and rapid mast cell degranulation. How is this hypersensitivity classified?
o: Type III immune complex deposition causing local vasculitis
Type II antibody-dependent cellular cytotoxic tissue damage
Type I immediate IgE-mediated allergic hypersensitivity reaction
Type IV delayed cell-mediated granulomatous inflammatory lesion
Type V stimulatory autoantibody receptor-binding pathology
qs.e: Type I hypersensitivity is mediated by IgE antibodies binding to mast cells, triggering rapid mediator release.
qs.s: Weekly Year 2: Cellular Immunology Exam - October 30, 2026 (Section A: MCQs)

qs.q: A 22-year-old woman presents with tender subcutaneous nodules on her shins and bilateral hilar adenopathy on chest radiography. A skin biopsy reveals non-caseating granulomas. This cell-mediated hypersensitivity reaction involves accumulation of which primary cell type?
o: Epithelioid macrophages together with activated T lymphocytes
Neutrophils combined directly with circulating immune complexes
Eosinophils recruited alongside IgE‑coated mucosal mast cells
Plasma cells proliferating alongside cytotoxic lymphocyte clones
Fibroblasts depositing a dense collagen‑rich extracellular matrix
qs.e: Sarcoidosis is characterized by non-caseating granulomas composed primarily of activated macrophages and CD4+ T helper cells.
qs.s: Weekly Pathology Exam - October 30, 2026 (Section A: MCQs)

qs.q: An HIV-positive patient initiating antiretroviral therapy develops a severe hypersensitivity reaction accompanied by a maculopapular rash shortly after taking non-nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitors. Which specific agent in this class is notorious for causing such hypersensitivity?
o: Zidovudine frequently causes this severe hypersensitivity
Tenofovir frequently causes this severe hypersensitivity
Raltegravir frequently causes this severe hypersensitivity
Nevirapine frequently causes this severe hypersensitivity
Ritonavir frequently causes this severe hypersensitivity
qs.e: Nevirapine frequently causes severe hypersensitivity reactions and hepatotoxicity, particularly during initiation therapy.

qs.q: A 26-year-old asthmatic patient complains of worsening cough and breathlessness triggered by house dust mites. Which hypersensitivity reaction type underlies this IgE-mediated response?
o: Type IV hypersensitivity reaction
Type II hypersensitivity reaction
Type I hypersensitivity reaction
Type III hypersensitivity reaction
qs.e: Allergenic triggers like house dust mites cause IgE-mediated reactions, which are classified as Type I hypersensitivity. Types II, III, and IV involve cytotoxic, immune complex, and delayed-type mechanisms respectively.
qs.s: Bronchial Asthma: Pathophysiology, Diagnosis and GINA Stepwise: MCQs

qs.q: A 9-year-old child with a history of myelomeningocele undergoes repeated bladder catheterizations and multiple surgical procedures during which they develop a sudden intraoperative hypersensitivity reaction. Which specific precaution should be standard practice in the care of all myelomeningocele patients to prevent this?
o: A. Using latex-free equipment
B. Performing routine amniocentesis
C. Maintaining a strict prone position
D. Providing oral folic acid
qs.e: Latex allergy is a well-recognized association in myelomeningocele patients due to repeated mucous membrane exposure, necessitating the use of latex-free equipment. Folic acid is used for prevention, not management of allergic reactions.
qs.s: Spina Bifida and Neural Tube Defects: Meningocele and Myelomeningocele: MCQs

qs.q: An industrial worker is diagnosed with a form of hypersensitivity pneumonitis driven by both immune complex deposition and cell-mediated immunity. Which combination of hypersensitivity reactions mediates this disease?
o: Type III and Type IV hypersensitivity reactions
Type I and Type II hypersensitivity reactions
Type II and Type III hypersensitivity reactions
Type I and Type IV hypersensitivity reactions
qs.e: Hypersensitivity pneumonitis involves both Type III immune complex reactions (with specific precipitating antibodies) and Type IV cell-mediated reactions. Type I is classic for acute allergic asthma rather than this condition.

qs.q: Which type of hypersensitivity reaction is primarily responsible for the circulation of immune complexes and their subsequent tissue deposition in systemic lupus erythematosus?
o: Type 4 hypersensitivity
Type 1 hypersensitivity
Type 3 hypersensitivity
Type 2 hypersensitivity
qs.e: Type 3 hypersensitivity involves the circulation of immune complexes that deposit in organs, leading to complement activation, inflammation, and tissue damage. The other hypersensitivity types involve different immunological mechanisms.

qs.q: When examining a skin biopsy from a patient with an acute hypersensitivity reaction to poison ivy, which histological hallmark is diagnostic of acute eczematous dermatitis?
o: Spongiosis, characterized by intercellular epidermal oedema splaying apart keratinocytes
Sparse superficial perivenular infiltrate of mononuclear cells with widened collagen bundles
Full-thickness epidermal necrosis extending down to the dermoepidermal junction
Subcorneal pustule formation packed tightly with neutrophilic inflammatory cells
qs.e: Spongiosis, or intercellular epidermal oedema that stretches intercellular bridges, is the histological hallmark of acute eczematous dermatitis. Subcorneal pustules are classic features of bacterial impetigo rather than dermatitis.
qs.s: Pathology of Acute Skin Inflammation: Urticaria & Eczema: MCQs

es.q: Outline the defining features, cellular components, and antibody type involved in Type I hypersensitivity reactions.
es.m:
- **Antibody type**: Involves the production of large amounts of IgE by atopic individuals.
- **Cellular components**: Involves mast cells, basophils, and eosinophils.
- **Antigens**: Characterized by antigens with low molecular weight and high solubility (allergens).
- **Alternative terms**: Also termed immediate hypersensitivity, anaphylactic reactions, or allergic reactions.
- **Timing**: Occurs within minutes to hours after exposure.
- **Phases**: Occurs in two phases: the sensitization phase (first contact) and the challenge phase (subsequent contact).

es.q: Discuss the features and clinical examples associated with Type II hypersensitivity reactions.
es.m:
- **Antibodies involved**: Mediated by IgG or IgM antibodies.
- **Target antigens**: Involves antigens bound to cell membranes (self antigens) or exogenous microbial antigens.
- **Complement activation**: Invariable complement activation occurs in this type of reaction.
- **Clinical examples**: Includes glomerulonephritis (anti-glomerular basement membrane) and mismatched blood transfusion.
- **Diagnosis**: Diagnosed by the detection of antibodies and antigens using immunofluorescence in tissue biopsy specimens such as the kidney or skin.

es.q: Describe the mechanism, tissue deposition sites, and clinical examples of Type III hypersensitivity reactions.
es.m:
- **Immune complex formation**: Occurs when an antigen reacts with an antibody (IgG or IgM) to form a soluble immune complex capable of inducing an inflammatory response.
- **Complement activation**: Involves complement activation that leads to the attraction of inflammatory cells.
- **Tissue deposition**: Immune complexes are deposited in tissues such as the kidneys, joints, or blood vessels.
- **Clinical examples**: Includes glomerulonephritis, rheumatoid arthritis, and systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE).
- **Diagnosis**: Diagnosed by the demonstration of specific immune complexes in the blood or tissues using immunofluorescence.

es.q: Outline the features and diagnostic methods of Type IV (delayed) hypersensitivity reactions.
es.m:
- **Immune mechanism**: Cell-mediated immune response involving antigen-dependent T cell (CD4 generally and CD8 occasionally) activation via MHC Class I or II.
- **Cellular components**: Involves activated macrophages and abnormal cellular response such as granuloma formation.
- **Timing**: Delayed onset occurring within 2 to 4 days, with an effector phase taking 24 to 72 hours and a sensitization phase of 1 to 2 weeks.
- **Clinical examples**: Includes allergic contact dermatitis and tuberculosis (TB) granuloma due to persistent antigen.
- **Diagnostic tests**: Diagnosed using the delayed skin test (Mantoux test), patch test (for contact dermatitis), and lymphocyte transformation test.

ai.summary: Hypersensitivity refers to exaggerated or inappropriate immune responses that cause tissue damage and disease. These reactions are classified into four main types (I-IV) based on the immune mechanism and timing. Understanding the specific type helps guide diagnosis and management to prevent severe outcomes.

sections.p: Hypersensitivity reactions are detrimental immune responses to otherwise harmless antigens, leading to tissue injury and disease. They are classified by the Gell and Coombs system into four types, each with distinct immunological mechanisms and clinical presentations. Diagnosis involves identifying the specific type of reaction and the causative antigen.
b: Type I (Immediate/Anaphylactic): IgE-mediated, rapid onset (minutes). Mast cell and basophil degranulation releases mediators like histamine.
Type II (Cytotoxic): IgG or IgM antibodies bind to cell surface antigens, leading to cell destruction via complement activation or antibody-dependent cellular cytotoxicity (ADCC).
Type III (Immune Complex): Soluble antigen-antibody complexes form in circulation, deposit in tissues, and activate complement, causing inflammation and tissue damage.
Type IV (Delayed-Type Hypersensitivity, DTH): T-cell mediated, typically manifesting 24-72 hours after antigen exposure. Involves sensitized T lymphocytes releasing cytokines.

sections.p: The severity of hypersensitivity reactions ranges from mild localized symptoms to life-threatening systemic responses. Staging is crucial for immediate management, especially for Type I reactions like anaphylaxis.
b: Mild: Localized skin reactions (urticaria, pruritus), mild rhinitis or conjunctivitis.
Moderate: Widespread urticaria, angioedema, mild bronchospasm, gastrointestinal symptoms (nausea, vomiting).

Severe (Anaphylaxis): Rapidly progressing, life-threatening systemic reaction involving multiple organ systems. Characterized by airway compromise (stridor, dyspnea), circulatory shock (hypotension), and severe skin/mucosal changes.
Chronic: Persistent inflammation and tissue damage, as seen in chronic hypersensitivity pneumonitis leading to fibrosis.

sections.p: Causes vary widely depending on the type of hypersensitivity, involving environmental, food, drug, and occupational exposures.
b: Type I: Pollen (e.g., goldenrod), dust mites, animal dander, insect venom, foods (e.g., milk in Heiner syndrome), drugs (e.g., penicillin). Often associated with atopy in childhood asthma, stimulated by IL-4 and IL-5.
Type II: Drug-induced hemolytic anemia (e.g., penicillin, quinidine), transfusion reactions, autoimmune hemolytic anemia, Rh incompatibility.
Type III: Serum sickness (e.g., animal antitoxins, some drugs), immune complex glomerulonephritis, Arthus reaction.

Type IV: Contact dermatitis (e.g., poison ivy, nickel), tuberculin skin test reaction, graft rejection, hypersensitivity pneumonitis (immune reaction to inhaled organic antigens like mouldy hay for farmer's lung, bird droppings for bird fancier's lung).
Occupational exposures for Type IV: Silica, asbestos, coal, certain drugs (amiodarone, methotrexate, nitrofurantoin, bleomycin), radiation.

sections.p: Clinical presentation is diverse, reflecting the specific immune mechanism and target tissues involved.
b: Type I: Rapid onset (minutes to hours) of urticaria, angioedema, pruritus, rhinitis, conjunctivitis, bronchospasm, abdominal pain, hypotension, or anaphylactic shock.
Type II: Hemolytic anemia (fatigue, pallor, jaundice), thrombocytopenia (purpura, bleeding), or neutropenia (infections). Symptoms depend on the affected cell type.
Type III: Manifests hours to days after exposure with fever, rash (urticarial or vasculitic), arthralgia, lymphadenopathy, and sometimes glomerulonephritis.

Type IV: Delayed onset (24-72 hours) with contact dermatitis (erythema, vesicles, pruritus), granulomas, or flu-like symptoms (fever, cough, dyspnea) in acute hypersensitivity pneumonitis. Chronic hypersensitivity pneumonitis can lead to progressive dyspnea and cough.

sections.p: Investigations aim to confirm hypersensitivity, identify the specific type, and pinpoint the causative allergen or antigen. Availability of tests may vary in low-resource settings, necessitating reliance on clinical history and physical examination.

t.b: Does the patient have IgE antibodies to specific allergens? A wheal and flare reaction indicates Type I hypersensitivity to that allergen. If unavailable, careful history of exposure and reaction is critical.
Are there circulating IgE antibodies to specific allergens? Elevated levels support Type I hypersensitivity. Useful when skin testing is contraindicated or unavailable.
Is there a delayed (Type IV) hypersensitivity reaction to a contact allergen? Erythema, papules, or vesicles at the site 48-72 hours after application indicate a positive reaction.

Are there signs of immune activation or cell destruction? Eosinophilia suggests Type I, II, or III. Anemia, thrombocytopenia, or neutropenia may suggest Type II. If unavailable, clinical signs of anemia or bleeding are important.
Is there complement consumption, suggesting immune complex (Type III) or cytotoxic (Type II) reactions? Decreased levels support these types.

What is the underlying tissue pathology? Histology can differentiate types (e.g., eosinophils in Type I, immune complex deposition in Type III, granulomas in Type IV). Essential for diagnosing conditions like hypersensitivity pneumonitis.

Is a specific substance truly causing the reaction? Carefully controlled exposure under medical supervision can confirm hypersensitivity, especially for foods or drugs. Reserved for specific situations due to risk.

sections.p: Prompt recognition of severe reactions is critical to prevent life-threatening complications and long-term organ damage.
b: Anaphylaxis: Rapid onset of airway obstruction (stridor, hoarseness), severe bronchospasm, hypotension, cardiovascular collapse. This is a medical emergency.
Angioedema of the airway: Swelling of the tongue, lips, or larynx, leading to respiratory compromise.
Organ damage: Acute kidney injury (Type III glomerulonephritis), lung fibrosis (chronic hypersensitivity pneumonitis), hemolytic crisis (Type II).
Shock: Profound hypotension and inadequate tissue perfusion, particularly in severe Type I reactions.

sections.p: Management focuses on immediate life support for severe reactions, identifying and avoiding the trigger, and modulating the immune response.
b: Emergency Management (Anaphylaxis): Administer epinephrine intramuscularly immediately. Secure airway, provide oxygen, intravenous fluids for hypotension. Antihistamines and corticosteroids are adjuncts.
Avoidance: Crucial for all types. Identify and eliminate exposure to the causative allergen/antigen. For Heiner syndrome, a milk-free diet is essential.
Antihistamines (e.g., H1 blockers like diphenhydramine, loratadine): Used for symptomatic relief of pruritus, urticaria, and rhinitis in Type I reactions. Chosen for efficacy and side effect profile.
Corticosteroids (e.g., prednisone, hydrocortisone): Reduce inflammation in Type I (severe), Type III, and Type IV reactions. Used systemically for severe cases or topically for localized reactions.

Immunosuppressants (e.g., methotrexate, azathioprine): May be used for chronic or severe Type III or Type IV reactions, such as severe hypersensitivity pneumonitis, when corticosteroids are insufficient or contraindicated.
Desensitization/Immunotherapy: Gradually introduce increasing doses of allergen to induce tolerance in selected Type I hypersensitivity cases (e.g., pollen, insect venom).
Supportive Care: Symptomatic treatment for rash, pain, fever. Monitor vital signs and organ function, especially in systemic reactions.

sections.p: Long-term management involves patient education, monitoring, and strategies to prevent future reactions.
b: Patient Education: Teach patients to recognize symptoms, avoid triggers, and use emergency medications (e.g., auto-injectable epinephrine).
Allergen Avoidance: Strict adherence to dietary restrictions (e.g., milk-free for Heiner syndrome), environmental controls (e.g., dust mite covers), or occupational safety measures.
Medical Alert Identification: Patients with severe allergies should wear medical alert bracelets or carry cards.
Regular Monitoring: For chronic conditions like hypersensitivity pneumonitis, regular pulmonary function tests and imaging are needed to monitor disease progression.
Pharmacological Prevention: Daily antihistamines for chronic allergic rhinitis, mast cell stabilizers (e.g., cromolyn) for some allergic conditions.

sections.p: Distinguishing hypersensitivity from other conditions with similar symptoms is vital for correct diagnosis and treatment.
b: Autoimmune Diseases: Both involve immune system dysregulation, but autoimmune diseases target self-antigens, while hypersensitivity targets external antigens.
Infections: Viral exanthems or bacterial toxins can cause rashes and systemic symptoms mimicking hypersensitivity reactions.
Drug Side Effects (Non-Allergic): Many drugs cause adverse reactions not mediated by the immune system (e.g., nausea, diarrhea, direct histamine release from opioids).
NASH (Non-alcoholic steatohepatitis): Comes with insulin resistance, not hypersensitivity, despite some shared inflammatory pathways.

sections.p: Interpreting diagnostic tests requires careful clinical correlation, as certain factors can lead to misleading results.
b: False Negative Skin Prick Test: Can occur if patient is on antihistamines, has poor skin reactivity, or if allergen extract potency is low.
False Positive Skin Prick Test: Irritant reactions, dermographism, or cross-reactivity with unrelated allergens can cause false positives.
Specific IgE Blood Test: Elevated levels indicate sensitization but not necessarily clinical allergy; many sensitized individuals do not react clinically.
Patch Test Interpretation: Requires expertise to differentiate irritant reactions from true allergic contact dermatitis. Reading too early or too late can miss reactions.
Challenge Tests: Risk of severe reaction, requiring careful patient selection and expert supervision. Negative challenge does not always rule out a rare or unusual reaction.

sections.p: Immediate medical attention is required for signs of a severe or rapidly worsening allergic reaction.
b: Difficulty breathing, wheezing, or stridor.
Swelling of the face, lips, tongue, or throat.
Sudden widespread rash or hives.
Dizziness, lightheadedness, or fainting.
Rapid heart rate or a sudden drop in blood pressure.
Severe abdominal pain, vomiting, or diarrhea after exposure.

faq.q: What is the main difference between allergy and hypersensitivity?
faq.a: Allergy is a common term for Type I hypersensitivity, specifically referring to IgE-mediated reactions. Hypersensitivity is a broader medical term encompassing all four types of exaggerated immune responses that cause tissue damage.

faq.q: Can hypersensitivity reactions change over time?
faq.a: Yes, hypersensitivity reactions can evolve. For example, childhood allergies may resolve, or new sensitivities can develop with repeated exposure. Chronic exposure in Type IV reactions can lead to irreversible tissue damage like fibrosis.

faq.q: Is it possible to be allergic to multiple things?
faq.a: Yes, it is common for individuals to be sensitized to multiple allergens, especially in Type I hypersensitivity. This is often seen in atopic individuals who may have allergic rhinitis, asthma, and food allergies.
